seriesTitle: The Reckoner of the Thirteenth Hour
title: Chapter 9: A Full Box, Still Warm
blurb: The night before the playoff, Drewe puts Mabry's full, warm box on Petra's desk and repeats the order that would hand Wardle a Pool Fraud Audit.

blocks.text: Whitlow read the east gate notice twice, standing at his window with my copy held out at arm's length. The second time through he yawned on Wardle's name, shut his mouth, and went on reading as if he hadn't.
'Why do you watch people's hands,' he said, 'when you're frightened?'
'Why do your clocks disagree?'
He did not answer, and neither did I. I put my pocket notebook on his table, open, and read him the four times, to the second, at which each of his clocks would next strike.
His face changed.

It was ten past nine in the morning. I had come from the night desk with the notice in my coat because it named two men, and I knew something about each of them that I could not tell him. Dunstan Mabry filled Drewe's snuffbox before every match. Felix Wardle had kept Marguerite spending on illegal paper for two seasons, then stopped renewing it and let it fall on her, and in the week it fell she had lain on the tram rails outside the Guild Hall with a tram coming. Now one of them paid for the Sleepless Hands and the other Reckoned them. In seven days I would stand across the Arbor from Wardle with our place in the League on the slates.

My verdict on Wardle was simple. A Reckoner who had kept one Sprinter on illegal paper, and now Reckoned for the man who filled Drewe's box, knew what a jar with someone else's seconds in it weighed. I had Reckoned five matchdays. I wanted someone who had Reckoned for years to tell me what a man like that would do. Whitlow was the only one I knew.

I had come the morning before to ask him. He had made tea, answered nothing, and fallen asleep in his chair with the cup in his hand. I took the cup from him. Then I sat at his table for an hour with his four clocks and my watch, which I set at the Regulator's stroke every night.

'The mantel clock,' I said now. 'Nine twenty-two and forty seconds. The one by the door, nine fifty-one and five. The left one on the dresser, ten-ten and thirty. The right one, ten-fifty and fifteen.' I turned the notebook round so he could read it. 'They strike twelve and nothing else. On the night you lent me your key they struck at those minutes. Yesterday they struck at those seconds. A clock left alone gains or loses a little every day. These haven't moved a minute in four weeks. Somebody keeps them wrong on purpose.'
Whitlow put both hands flat on the table, either side of my notebook. They were broad, old hands, with ink in the creases of the right forefinger. They did not move.
'Leave them be,' he said.
'What are they for?'
'What are you for, that you sit in an old man's flat for an hour and do that with it?'
I did not answer that either. At twenty-two minutes and forty seconds past nine by my watch, the mantel clock struck twelve. He did not look at it. He looked at me.
Under the foot of each clock lay a Bank envelope with its flap tucked in. I had seen them the day before. I had not touched them, and I did not touch them now. I told him what I had instead.

'The printed Laws say Deferral and Assumption were banned in the Reform, thirty-one years ago. Paper deferred before the Reform is Old Paper. Its holder may still roll it legally, as long as he pays at least the interest every week. A weekly roll falls due at a set time.' I looked at the clocks, and then back at his hands. 'Four clocks. Four envelopes. Four times. You're rolling Old Paper.'

That much was the Laws and the clocks. My verdict was my own, and I kept it to myself. He had run the paper up himself, in whatever he had played before he Reckoned, and he had been too proud for thirty-one years to let anyone see the bill.
He yawned in the middle of breathing out and turned it into a sigh.

'Cold paper,' he said. 'All four.' He took his hands off the table and folded them in his lap. 'One of them's mine. The other three I Assumed, the week before the Reform, from three men I played with at the Ash Hours. Nineteen days of stall, the four together. Each one was written on a different night, so each one's week runs out at a different minute. The clock strikes twelve when it does. Twelve, and I've paid that week's interest, or I haven't.'
'I thought you'd run it all up yourself,' I said. 'I was wrong.'
'A quarter right.'
'Three-quarters wrong. Three of the four aren't yours.' I looked at the envelopes. 'How do you pay it?'
'In my sleep. Every night.'

I did the sum on the page in front of him, because I wanted to see it written down. Three per cent a week on nineteen days is thirteen hours and forty-one minutes of stall a week, a little under two hours a night. More than two hours of stall in one night's sleep leaves a sleeper stall-sick the next day. He had kept three minutes under that line every night for thirty-one years. In that time he had served about two and a half years of stall in his sleep, and he still owed every minute of the nineteen days.
'That's why you yawn,' I said.
'I don't yawn.'
'If you stop paying, the whole nineteen days fall due at once. They won't fit in a Week of Grace, so you'd serve them as one stall. Nineteen days, wherever you happened to be.'
'I know what it would cost.'
'There's no other way out of Old Paper in the Laws. I've read them.'
'You've read the printed Laws.' He picked up his cup, found it empty, and set it down again. 'The printed Laws are not the whole Laws.'
'What does that mean?'
'It means what it says.'
'What isn't printed?'

He shook his head, slowly, once. He did not look sorry, and he did not look like a man who would change his mind. I have read every printed page of the Laws of Lull, and I do not guess at the rest. I wrote down what he had said, word for word, under the clock times, because he was not a man who said things by accident.
'I could go through the envelopes with you,' I said. 'There might be a—'

'No.' He said it kindly. 'I've not asked anyone to carry it in thirty-one years. I'll not start with the one who's carrying the Ninth Stair.' He nodded at the notice on the windowsill. 'You came about Wardle.'
'I want to know what he'll do.'
'Who stood on his plates for two seasons?'
'Marguerite.'
'Then why are you asking me?' He yawned again, and this time he let it finish. 'Ask her if he kept his slates. The careful ones do.'
On the stairs down past the locksmith's I heard the clock by the door strike twelve behind me. I did not look at my watch. I knew what it would say.
Marguerite came to the landing at six with a sack over her shoulder that clanked when she set it down.

Bao was already asleep on the bench under the Rate Board with his cap over his eyes. He had paid the three hours and fifty-one minutes that fell due after MD11, which put him back at twenty-three and a half on my sheet, and he was paying more on top of it wherever he could lie down. Drewe sat at the other end of the bench, turning her screwdriver over in her fingers.
I had asked Marguerite at the Guild door that afternoon whether Wardle kept his slates. She had looked at me for a long moment, said, 'Wait there,' and gone. This was what she had gone for.
The sack held roof slates, nineteen of them, each about the size of a ledger, each scratched with a nail in a column of twelve numbers.

'He did his bids in chalk like everybody,' Marguerite said. 'Then after the match he scratched them on these and hung them on nails on our landing. Said a Reckoner who rubs his bids out is lying to himself.' She crouched and laid them out in rows on the boards. 'When the Copper folded I took them down. Nobody else wanted them.'
She had kept them for a year, in a sack, and said nothing about them. My verdict, which I kept to myself: she had kept them in case she ever needed something to hold over him.
'Why did you keep them?' I said.

Marguerite sat back on her heels. 'Because they're the only thing he ever gave me that was true. I could look at them and know what had happened.' She pushed a slate straight with one finger. 'Two coppers says you thought it was blackmail.'
'I did. I was wrong.'
It was the first bet she had made since the MD11 Close. I had not taken it, but she held her hand out, and I paid her. Bao lifted his cap an inch to watch, and put it back.

I read the slates one figure at a time, the way I read a jar. Nineteen matches, two hundred and twenty-eight bids. Marguerite told me, slate by slate, what she had been issued and what she had spent, and she remembered more of it than I expected.

'He tots up our weeks before every match,' she said. 'What each of us could stand in stalls. Whatever we couldn't afford to spend, he banked. Every Bank minute. He'd sooner a second sat in the chamber than in a Sprinter who couldn't pay for it.'
'Except you.'
'Except me.' She did not look up. 'I could always afford it. That was what the paper was for.'

The slates showed the other half of him. Wardle lost a bank point forty-one times in nineteen matches. Thirty-eight of those times his next slate was higher than the one that lost, by ten seconds or more, and every second of the rise came out of what he could issue that round. He did not like losing a bank point. He liked it less than losing a run.
'Lose him a point, he winds himself up,' Drewe said. 'Proper mainspring, that one.'
Marguerite nodded at her as if it had been a fair point and not a pun.

'So we make him chase,' I said. 'Early. I read his first slates the way I read Coyle's and the Chandler's Stair man's, and I take the early bank points by a few seconds. He banks higher to win them back. Every second he chases with goes into the locked chamber, and it stays there until the Close. By the late rounds his Sprinters have less to run on than he planned for.'
'And ours?' Marguerite said.
'We bank too. Less than him, and only where it wins. You'll run less early and more late.'
'Two coppers says he's chasing by round three.'
Nobody took it.
From under the cap, Bao said, 'Mm. Long Keep, then.'
'A long Keep. Can you hold it?'
'Rest assured,' Bao said, and went back to sleep.
Drewe laughed out loud. Marguerite threw a glove at her, and missed, and it landed on Bao, who did not wake.

I put the slates back in the sack myself. I had one more verdict, and I did not say it on the landing: Mabry did not pay for a side he was not also filling. If the Sleepless Hands' jar ran short in the late rounds and their Sprinters kept running anyway, the seconds would be coming from somewhere.
Then I asked them what they would carry.

I had decided on the walk from Whitlow's that I would not choose it for them. A Stall Book is written at the Close, line by line, from what I issued, with each debtor's spoken consent. But what a player is willing to owe is hers to say before the match, not mine to discover after it. I put my notebook on the bench and told them so.

Marguerite went first. 'Two hundred and forty. Not a second over. All of it in my three o'clocks, same as always.' She looked at the sack. 'And I run the far starts. He watched me two seasons. He knows I like a near start and a short carry. I'll give him the long way round.'
'The far starts cost more.'
'I know what they cost. I'm choosing it.' If I needed more than two hundred and forty from her, she said, I was to ask her on the plate, out loud, and she would answer me yes or no.
I wrote it down as she said it. Two hundred and forty, into her three o'clocks. Far starts. Anything over, asked aloud.
Drewe turned the screwdriver end over end and caught it.

'I go to the pickup,' she said. 'Night before, like always. If I don't, he knows. If he knows, he finds somebody who isn't me to stand next to you lot, and I'd rather it was me.' She caught the screwdriver again. 'I carry it on to the landing. I wind what you issue and nothing else. Friction into my half-past-ones, if you'll have it.'
'A box on the landing is a lifetime ban if an Arbiter finds it,' I said.
'I know what it is. It's mine to carry.'

It was. I had told her so myself, at my desk, with the box warm in my hand. I wrote that down too, under Marguerite's: issued seconds only, friction into her half-past-ones, and the box her own choice.
Drewe went to her last pickup the night before the playoff.

She came up to the Guild night desk at a quarter to eleven. I heard her on the stair before I saw her, and she was not whistling. She put the snuffbox on my blotter and laid her hands flat on either side of it.
'Full,' she said. 'Warm. Card's in the lid.'
I opened the lid. The card said what Mabry's cards always said: wind times, in his round copybook letters, and nothing else. I closed it again.
'He gave me a sugared almond,' Drewe said. 'Asked after my mum's knee. Didn't ask why the last one came back full. Then he told me what this one's for.'
I was afraid.

Her hands did not move. There was a smear of clock oil on the left thumb, and the nails were bitten short, which they had not been last week. The screwdriver was in her coat pocket. I could see the end of it.

'He wants it wound into you lot,' she said. 'All of it, in live play, and none of it spent. Left in their hands till the round ends, so it goes back in the jar. When it's in, I touch my collar. Then Mr Wardle calls his Audit in the next Bank minute.' She looked at the box and not at me. 'He says it's a little arrangement, my dear. He says the Queue's been waiting long enough.'

If the Arbiter weighed our jar over Issue minus Tally, it was Pool Fraud, the playoff was forfeit, and the Ninth Stair would be disbanded and our keys suspended for a year; Mabry had written none of it down, and the hands he had chosen to do it with were lying flat on my desk, either side of a full box, not shaking.
